newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Agencies send some aid to Rwanda refugees in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Agencies send some aid to Rwanda refugees in Zaire.

text.p: U.N. agencies managed to send some aid on Tuesday to thousands of Rwandan refugees emerging from hiding in Zaire's forests but had some problems with rebel cooperation.

The rebels failed the first test on Monday of rebel leader Laurent Kabila's promise on Sunday of free access to refugees when an aid convoy was turned back at a checkpoint at Biaro, 41 km (25 miles) south of the northeastern capital of Kisangani.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said out of 21 sick refugees driven out of Biaro camp on Monday, one had died and two were having limbs amputated on Tuesday because of gangrenous wounds.

"It seems today the (rebel) alliance is requiring escorts and limiting the number of aid vehicles allowed south of Kisangani," said UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg. "These are not the arrangements which we agreed with the governor last night."
He said UNHCR heard it would not be allowed to fly the 21 refugees from Kisangani to Gisenyi in Rwanda and it was also in doubt whether refugees could go to a hospital near Kisangani.

He said of 11 UNHCR trucks loaded with blankets, jerry cans, plastic sheeting, milk, soap and biscuits, only three were allowed to head south while the others were told to wait for a rebel train bringing refugees back to the northeastern capital.
But an official at the railway station said the refugees would be dropped at Biaro and not taken by train to Kisangani.
"This is not the plan agreed. It is a coordination problem," Stromberg said.
The U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said it was relatively satisfied by access to refugees allowed on Tuesday.

A WFP spokeswoman said five WFP food trucks were permitted to drive south of Kisangani and the city's large international airport was opened to aid flights on Tuesday for the first time since it fell to rebels in March and mines were cleared.

Before they were turned back on Monday, aid workers and journalists saw some 5,000 Hutu refugees emerge from the forests and return to Biaro, which they said they fled last week after being attacked by villagers and the Tutsi-dominated rebels.
Aid workers said up to 10,000 arrived at Biaro by Tuesday.
The condition of the refugees shocked even aid officials hardened by years of dealing with the Rwandan refugee crisis.
Dozens of those emerging from the forest were desperately ill -- many with cholera, doctors said -- and others bore horrific wounds from the attacks that sparked their exodus.

Rebel authorities have denied attacking camps at Kasese and Biaro last week. They said rebels intervened and were ambushed by Rwandan militiamen among the refugees only after villagers attacked the camps in retaliation for the killing of six Zairean civilians by refugees.
A bid by rebels to portray themselves as caring for refugees was dismissed by another aid official as "a cynical charade".

Two rebels, clad in fresh uniforms, emerged from the camp wearing surgical gloves and saying they had been helping the refugees for five days. One spent most of his time shooing away refugees during Monday's visit by aid workers and journalists.
The Hutu refugees appeared terrified. One priority for aid workers was to bury the dozens of bodies in the camps.
More than 30 were seen on Monday. Some, aid officials said, had died of illness while others had been brutally attacked.
The stench of decaying corpses blew in from deeper within the jungle and refugees emerging from the forest reported seeing hundreds of bodies there.
The 85,000 Hutu refugees from Kasese and Biaro were among up to 100,000 south of Kisangani missing since aid agencies and journalists were barred from the camps by rebels last week.
The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda in 1994 and are collectively accused by minority Tutsis of genocide in Rwanda the same year.
An outbreak of cholera was cited by rebels as the reason for delaying the start of a planned U.N. airlift of the refugees.

Kabila demanded on Sunday that aid agencies repatriate all the remaining Rwandan refugees in Zaire within 60 days. The United States, UNHCR and U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan say the deadline is unrealistic.
Aid workers say it is impossible to repatriate all 100,000 south of Kisangani and another 250,000 Rwandan refugees who are still unaccounted for in Zaire even with full rebel cooperation.
